atlas-ee.0113: Outside the quota: highly skilled ICT workers, people working for start-ups, students and academics, and top specialists paid at least 1.5 times the average wage. Employers pay at least the average gross salary, €2,092 a month from 5 March 2026 (a 0.8 rate of €1,674 is listed).
atlas-ee.0114: Raise it at the first interview: an employer who knows the exempt routes can move fast, one who does not will think of the three-week advert and the quota. EU and EEA citizens need no permit.
atlas-ee.0115: Portals: Work in Estonia (English-language offers, state agency), CV.ee, CV Keskus and MeetFrank for tech; EURES Estonia for people coming from Europe; the TalTech career portal for students.
atlas-ee.0116: Employer pages: Wise (wise.jobs), Bolt (bolt.eu careers), Swedbank Kick Start, Cybernetica interns, Luminor and SEB Youth LAB summer internships, Coop Pank and Telia summer placements.
atlas-ee.0117: Expat Facebook groups for jobs in Tallinn are listed by Work in Estonia; we found no graduate-fair listing beyond the university career days.
atlas-ee.0118: Treating the placement as optional: where the degree requires it, it is the entry, and the competition is real (about 4% of Telia’s applicants placed).
atlas-ee.0119: Sending one generic letter: students report writing a separate cover letter for each application.
atlas-ee.0120: Assuming English is enough everywhere: it is in software and start-ups, but banks, audit teams and the public sector work in Estonian, and a permit extension after five years needs Estonian at A2.
atlas-ee.0121: Reading sector averages as entry pay: the lowest tenth of ICT employees earned under €1,246 a month in 2025.
atlas-ee.0122: Software start-ups and scale-ups hire in English: Work in Estonia’s board lists Bolt (105), Wise (58) and Playtech (13) offers on 8 October 2026; the evidence is the interview and a home task, and no language certificate is mentioned.
atlas-ee.0123: Research and joint projects at Tartu run in English (the industrial master’s, the Bolt autonomous-driving lab); we found no employer page that asks for a language level.
atlas-ee.0124: Cybersecurity is tied to the state (CR14, NATO’s Tallinn centre, Cybernetica), where Estonian matters for state work; no page we read states a level.
atlas-ee.0125: Banks work in English and Estonian: some Luminor teams need Estonian as well as English, and the fintechs hire in English. Employers test through the interview; we found no certificate requirement.
atlas-ee.0126: Audit and accounting assistants need Estonian for client work as well as English; a Big Four audit-intern advert listed English and Estonian as the languages.
atlas-ee.0127: Scale-ups hire business graduates in English; marketing, sales and most other business jobs are in Estonian or Russian.
atlas-ee.0128: The state works in Estonian; the one language rule we read is that a permit holder needs Estonian at level A2 to extend after five years.
atlas-ee.0129: In 2025, 91.0% of tertiary graduates aged 20–34 who finished within the last three years were in work (EU 85.3%), but youth unemployment (15–24) was 20.7%, up from 17.3% in 2023; the entry door is narrow rather than shut.
atlas-ee.0130: No national figure for the share of interns who are kept: Telia placed about 4% of its applicants, Coop Pank looks to its interns first, and 65% of TalTech’s foreign IT students had work in their field.
atlas-ee.0131: EU, EEA and Swiss citizens may work from day one; the employer enters you in the employment register before you start.
atlas-ee.0132: Within three months, register your address with the municipality: you get a personal code and a five-year right of residence. Within a month after that, apply for the ID card, €45.
atlas-ee.0134: Issued for the full nominal length of the course. Students may work without an hourly limit, as long as the studies stay on track.
atlas-ee.0135: The permit gives no public health cover: you need private insurance until a job with social tax makes you insured.
atlas-ee.0136: A non-EU student with a study permit from another EU country can study here up to 360 days with no Estonian visa or permit.
atlas-ee.0143: For students abroad or graduates of the last two years: the host registers the traineeship with the police, then you get a D visa for up to 365 days, with a three-party training agreement. Interns studying in Estonia are covered by their study permit.
atlas-ee.0146: After a degree in Estonia you may stay 270 days to find work or start a company, and work full time meanwhile.
atlas-ee.0147: An Estonian graduate who is hired skips the quota, the labour-market test and the average-salary rule: the minimum wage, €946 a month, is enough.
atlas-ee.0148: The 270 days hold only inside Estonia: with an expired card you cannot travel in Schengen and come back.
atlas-ee.0149: EU Blue Card, top specialist, ICT and start-up routes
atlas-ee.0150: All four are outside the quota and need no labour-market test, and family can come at once.
atlas-ee.0151: The Blue Card needs a contract of six months and a degree or three years of experience in the last seven; ICT roles need only the average wage; start-ups certified by Startup Estonia may pay the minimum wage.
atlas-ee.0152: Salary, Blue Card and top specialist
atlas-ee.0154: Salary, Blue Card in shortage or STEM roles
atlas-ee.0160: The employer registers the job with the police; no quota and no labour-market test, but the pay must reach the Estonian average wage and the company must have traded for six months. Up to 365 days in any 455, then 90 days away.
atlas-ee.0162: Needs a labour-market test by Töötukassa (three weeks of advertising) and a place in the yearly quota of 1,292, which usually runs out in the first weeks of the year. Employers often use short-term employment first.
atlas-ee.0163: After five years on this permit, renewal needs Estonian at A2.
atlas-ee.0164: A hosting agreement with an institution in the ETIS register; outside the quota, no labour-market test, family at once.
atlas-ee.0165: Since 2022 PhD students are hired as junior research fellows on four-year contracts, with salary, public health cover and pension.
atlas-ee.0166: €225 in Estonia, €255 at an embassy; D visa €120
atlas-ee.0167: Estonia’s working-holiday agreements are only with Australia, New Zealand, Canada and Japan.
atlas-ee.0168: For citizens of the partner countries aged 18 to 30 (Canada 18 to 35): a D visa for 12 months, outside the quota.
atlas-ee.0169: Up to 90 days in any 180. Visa-free visitors may work only if the employer has registered short-term employment first.
atlas-ee.0170: Bring a valid passport or ID card and your European Health Insurance Card, which covers you until you are insured locally. You may work from day one; your employer must enter you in the employment register before you start.
atlas-ee.0171: For a first job, employers usually register short-term employment and you apply for a D visa (€120) at an Estonian embassy or visa centre: the temporary residence permit route is often closed by the annual quota.
atlas-ee.0172: Staying over 3 months, register your residence in the population register within 3 months of arriving, at the local government office or the International House of Estonia in Tallinn, with your lease. It is done on the spot and starts your 5-year right of residence.
atlas-ee.0173: After arriving, register your address in the population register, and make sure your employer has entered you in the employment register before your first day of work.
atlas-ee.0174: Within 1 month of registering, apply at a Police and Border Guard office (book at broneering.politsei.ee) for the Estonian ID card for EU citizens: €45, ready in 10 to 15 working days.
atlas-ee.0175: A temporary residence permit comes as a biometric residence card (elamisloakaart); a student permit costs €225 if you apply in Estonia, €255 at an embassy, decided within 2 months.
atlas-ee.0176: Registering in the population register gives you the Estonian personal identification code (isikukood), used for tax, health and every digital service.
atlas-ee.0177: Public health cover (Tervisekassa) starts when your employer pays social tax for you, after a 14-day waiting period from your entry in the employment register.
atlas-ee.0178: Until then, and as a student, your European Health Insurance Card covers you.
atlas-ee.0179: A study permit does not give public cover: keep compliant private insurance (ERGO, Inges, Swisscare) of at least €30,000 for the whole stay, unless you are employed.
atlas-ee.0180: High-street banks charge newcomers a non-refundable identity-check fee of up to €250; your employer must accept a European IBAN (Wise, Revolut) for your pay. With an Estonian ID card, an account at LHV or Swedbank opens online for free.
atlas-ee.0181: The ID card is your digital ID: use it with the DigiDoc4 software and a card reader, then set up the Smart-ID app to log in and sign legally from your phone.
atlas-ee.0182: Your right of residence depends on a valid address in the population register: register a new flat within 30 days of moving, or the right lapses, and with it your health cover.
